docs.title: Dynatrace AI Agent Workshop
docs.text:
AI agents are evolving fast, but many organizations still struggle with rising costs, limited visibility, and unreliable performance in production.

In this hands-on workshop you'll design, deploy, and optimize cost-efficient AI agent workflows using BMAD, kagent, Kubernetes, and Dynatrace AI Observability — all from a single GitHub Codespace.

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
• Control the biggest driver of AI agent costs.
  • Build structured multi-agent workflows with BMAD.
  • Deploy AI agents on Kubernetes using kagent.
  • Secure agents with Tetragon and Agent Sandbox.
  • Monitor cost, performance, and efficiency with Dynatrace AI Observability.
  • Evaluate agents with Phoenix + dt-evals, then optimize the inefficient ones.

docs.title: Workshop arc
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Why[Why: cost & visibility] --> Kagent[kagent runtime]
    Kagent --> Cluster[Build cluster]
    Cluster --> Deploy[Deploy agents]
    Deploy --> Secure[Secure]
    Secure --> Observe[Observe]
    Observe --> Evaluate[Evaluate]
    Evaluate --> Optimize[Optimize]
  1. Why — cost, visibility, reliability of AI agents in production.
  2. kagent intro — the agentic runtime on Kubernetes.
  3. Build the cluster (Codespace).
  4. Deploy two agent sets — an SRE agent + the BMAD software-building crew.
  5. Secure agents — Tetragon runtime security + Agent Sandbox.
  6. Observe — Dynatrace AI Observability.
  7. Evaluate — Phoenix (Arize) + dt-evals.
  8. Optimize — find unused tools/skills and cut token spend.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
New to kagent? Read kagent in 5 minutes for the mental model, then head to 00 — Setup (Codespace) to boot your environment. The modules run in order:

  1. kagent in 5 minutes — the runtime, in one page.
  2. 00 — Setup (Codespace) — boot the cluster.
  3. 01 — Platform install — operators, kagent, Tetragon, Phoenix.
  4. 02 — Agents & MCP wiring — deploy the SRE agent + BMAD crew.
  5. 03 — Secure agents — Tetragon + Agent Sandbox.
  6. 04 — Observe with Dynatrace — cost, tokens, latency.
  7. 05 — Diagnose a broken cluster — inject a fault, let the agent find the root cause.
  8. 06 — Evaluate (Phoenix + dt-evals) — score quality + cost.
  9. 07 — Optimize — cut the waste, keep the quality.

Running the live demo? The Run of show (guided demo) stitches these modules into one top-to-bottom 13-step script — configure an agent, investigate the cluster, turn on observability, evaluate, and optimize — with a link back to each module for the depth behind every step.

Stuck anywhere? The Troubleshooting page collects the common fixes per module.

This site is built with MkDocs Material and served from the Codespace on forwarded port 8000 (mkdocs serve -a 0.0.0.0:8000).

docs.title: 00 — Setup (Codespace)
docs.text:
This module gets you from zero to a running local Kubernetes cluster inside a GitHub Codespace, with the full workshop toolchain installed.

Start here first

If you haven't forked the repo and created your tokens yet, begin with Start the benchmark — it walks fork → Codespace → secrets end to end. This module is the detailed Codespace reference.

docs.title: 1. Open the Codespace
docs.text:
1. On your fork, click Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main.
  2. Machine type: choose 4-core / 16 GB or larger. The default 2-core/4GB is not enough for the full stack (see .devcontainer/DECISIONS.md).

The devcontainer builds, then postCreate automatically:

  • verifies the toolchain (kubectl, helm, kind, k3d, kagent, uv, mkdocs),
  • creates a local Kubernetes cluster (k3d by default),
  • stages namespaces + Helm repos for the platform install,
  • reports which secrets are present.

docs.title: 2. Configure secrets
docs.text:
All required tokens — what each is, the exact permissions, and where to create each one — live on a single page: Start the benchmark → Create the required tokens. Set them as Codespace secrets (scoped to your fork) as described there, then rebuild or restart the Codespace. Full machine-readable contract: .devcontainer/SECRETS.md.

Verify presence (values are never printed):

bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/check-secrets.sh

docs.title: 3. Verify the cluster
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get namespaces

You should see a Ready node and the staged namespaces (dynatrace, kagent, tetragon, phoenix, …).

docs.title: 4. Re-running the bootstrap (idempotent)
docs.text:
Everything is safe to re-run:

bash .devcontainer/postCreate.sh     # full bootstrap (reuses an existing cluster)
bash .devcontainer/postStart.sh      # restart the cluster after a resume

docs.title: 5. Serve this site locally
docs.text:
mkdocs serve -a 0.0.0.0:8000

Open the forwarded port 8000.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Phase 2 installs the platform (Dynatrace Operator, OpenTelemetry Operator, kagent, Tetragon, Agent Sandbox, Phoenix).

docs.title: 01 — Platform install
docs.text:
With the Codespace cluster running (module 00), install the observability + agent platform. Everything lives under cluster/ and installs with one idempotent script.

What gets installed

Dynatrace Operator (Kubernetes monitoring), OpenTelemetry Operator + a gateway collector, kagent (clean base — no agents yet), Tetragon (eBPF security), an Agent Sandbox isolation baseline, and Phoenix (LLM eval/trace UI).

docs.title: 1. Set your secrets
docs.text:
The install reads secrets from the environment (see SECRETS.md). Set these as Codespace secrets and rebuild/restart:

Secret Used by DT_TENANT_URL Dynatrace Operator + OTLP export DT_API_TOKEN Dynatrace Operator + OTLP export LLM_API_KEY (or OPENAI_API_KEY) kagent model provider (needed in Phase 3)

Missing secrets degrade gracefully — a component is skipped or warns, the install never crashes.

docs.title: 2. Run the install
docs.text:
bash cluster/install.sh

Re-runnable any time (helm upgrade --install + kubectl apply). Skip a component with, e.g., INSTALL_DYNATRACE=false bash cluster/install.sh.

docs.title: 3. Verify (acceptance)
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A                                   # all operators/components Ready
kubectl get dynakube -n dynatrace                     # Dynatrace k8s monitoring
kubectl get otelcol -n opentelemetry-operator-system  # gateway collector
kubectl -n kagent get pods                            # kagent controller/ui/kmcp/db
kubectl -n tetragon get pods                          # Tetragon DaemonSet
kubectl -n phoenix get pods                           # Phoenix

Open Phoenix on the forwarded port 6006. Open the kagent UI with:

kubectl -n kagent port-forward svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080

docs.title: How telemetry flows
docs.text:
kagent agents / instrumented workloads
      │ OTLP 4317/4318
      ▼
 otel-gateway-collector ──▶ Dynatrace tenant (OTLP ingest)   — observe
      (ns opentelemetry-    └▶ Phoenix :4317                  — eval/trace UI
       operator-system)

The gateway normalises OpenInference/Traceloop LLM attributes to OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* semconv so Dynatrace and Phoenix agree on names. There are no agents yet — kagent is a clean base; module 02 (Phase 3) deploys the SRE agent and the BMAD crew, at which point spans start landing in both backends.

BindPlane

BindPlane (OTel collector management) is illustrated, not installed — see the walkthrough.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Tetragon not Ready — eBPF/BTF on the Codespace kernel; see cluster/tetragon/README.md.
  • OTel operator hangs — it must use its self-signed webhook cert (autoGenerateCert), already set in otel/operator-values.yaml.
  • No data in Dynatrace — check DT_TENANT_URL/DT_API_TOKEN and token scopes (openTelemetryTrace.ingest, metrics.ingest, logs.ingest).

docs.title: 02 — Agents & MCP wiring
docs.text:
With the platform up (module 01), wire MCP tooling into kagent and deploy the two agent sets. Everything lives under agents/ and installs with one idempotent script.

What gets deployed

A shared workshop-llm ModelConfig (DeepSeek, OpenAI-API compatible), the GitHub and Dynatrace MCP tool servers, an SRE agent, and the six-member BMAD crew. kagent's built-in kagent-tool-server (default Kubernetes tooling) is turned on for this phase.

docs.title: The tool surfaces
docs.text:
Tool Source Agent Kubernetes / kubectl + k8s-networking built-in kagent-tool-server SRE Dynatrace (problems, entities, logs/DQL, metrics, Davis) dynatrace-mcp-remote SRE GitHub (issues, PRs, repo contents) github-mcp-remote BMAD crew

All agents share one model: workshop-llm — DeepSeek (deepseek-chat, DeepSeek-V3), chosen for the workshop's cost-efficiency theme. DeepSeek's API is OpenAI-compatible, so kagent's OpenAI provider is pointed at https://api.deepseek.com/v1 and reads the key from secret/kagent-deepseek. Swap to OpenAI or Anthropic in agents/mcp/00-modelconfig.yaml (one-line change).

docs.title: 1. Enable the default Kubernetes tooling
docs.text:
Phase 2 shipped kagent as a clean base with the built-in tools off. Phase 3 turns them on (already set in cluster/kagent/values.yaml):

kagent-tools: { enabled: true }   # built-in kagent-tool-server (k8s + networking)

If you installed the platform before this change, re-run bash cluster/install.sh to roll kagent and create the kagent-tool-server.

docs.title: 2. Provide the MCP credentials
docs.text:
These are injected at apply time and never committed. You created them during onboarding — see Start the benchmark → Create the required tokens for the exact permissions and where each is generated:

Variable Used by Notes GH_PAT GitHub MCP Fine-grained PAT scoped to the one demo repo: Contents RW · Issues RW · Pull requests RW. No org/admin. (token E) DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN Dynatrace MCP Dynatrace platform token (dt0s16.*) — distinct from the Phase-2 OTLP DT_API_TOKEN. (token B) DT_ENVIRONMENT Dynatrace MCP Platform apps URL, e.g. https://abc12345.apps.dynatrace.com. Derived from DT_TENANT_URL (.live.→.apps.) if unset. 
export GH_PAT='github_pat_...'
export DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN='dt0s16....'
export DT_ENVIRONMENT='https://<env>.apps.dynatrace.com'

Token in pod env

The GitHub/Dynatrace MCP servers receive their token as a pod env var (kagent's MCPServer env is a static map). Scope the tokens tightly and rotate them after the workshop.

docs.title: 3. Install
docs.text:
bash agents/install-agents.sh

The script applies, in order: the MCP layer (ModelConfig + GitHub + Dynatrace), the SRE agent, then the BMAD crew.

docs.title: 4. Verify the tools registered
docs.text:
kubectl -n kagent get mcpserver,remotemcpserver
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver kagent-tool-server  -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver github-mcp-remote    -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver dynatrace-mcp-remote -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get agents

Each RemoteMCPServer should be Accepted with a non-empty discoveredTools list, and all seven agents (sre-agent + six bmad-*) should be Accepted.

docs.title: 5. Send a sample prompt
docs.text:
SRE agentBMAD orchestrator 
kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List the pods in the kagent namespace and tell me if any are unhealthy."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/sre-agent

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Build a simple Todo app in <owner>/<repo>. Run the full BMAD workflow and open a PR."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/bmad-orchestrator

Or use the kagent UI: kubectl -n kagent port-forward svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080.

docs.title: 6. See the traces
docs.text:
Agent LLM and tool-call spans flow automatically (kagent otel.tracing, wired in Phase 2) through the OTel gateway to both backends:

  • Phoenix — http://localhost:6006 (forwarded Codespace port) for LLM eval/trace inspection.
  • Dynatrace — distributed traces on your tenant.

That satisfies the acceptance for this phase: both agent sets respond to a sample prompt, and their traces land in Phoenix and Dynatrace.

docs.title: 03 — Secure agents (Tetragon + Agent Sandbox)
docs.text:
An AI agent is, by design, given tools and told to act. That is exactly what makes it useful — and exactly what makes it risky. A prompt-injected or mis-behaving agent will happily run whatever tool it can reach. This module adds two independent layers of defence that were installed in module 01:

  • Agent Sandbox — contain where an agent can go (namespace isolation).
  • Tetragon — observe and optionally enforce what an agent's processes do at runtime (eBPF).

Defence in depth

Neither layer replaces the other. The sandbox is a static boundary (admission + network policy); Tetragon is a runtime sensor that sees the actual syscalls/exec/network events — and can kill on policy violation. Use both.

docs.title: Part A — Agent Sandbox (isolation baseline)
docs.text:
The agent-sandbox namespace ships a self-contained isolation baseline — no external project required. It lives in cluster/agent-sandbox/isolation.yaml and enforces two things on anything scheduled into it:

Control What it does Pod Security Admission restricted Pods must run non-root, drop ALL Linux capabilities, forbid privilege escalation, and use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile. Default-deny NetworkPolicy All ingress is blocked; egress is allowed only to DNS (port 53) and the OTel gateway (4317/4318) — so a sandboxed agent can still be observed but cannot roam the cluster or call out to the internet.

docs.title: Verify the sandbox
docs.text:
# PSA labels enforce the "restricted" profile
kubectl get ns agent-sandbox -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'; echo

# the default-deny policy is present
kubectl -n agent-sandbox get networkpolicy

You should see pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted in the labels and a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Prove it actually blocks
docs.text:
Try to schedule a privileged, root pod into the sandbox — admission must reject it:

kubectl -n agent-sandbox run rogue --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"rogue","image":"busybox:1.36","securityContext":{"privileged":true,"runAsUser":0},"command":["sleep","3600"]}]}}' \
  --command -- sleep 3600

Expected

The API server refuses the pod with a violates PodSecurity "restricted" error (privileged, runAsUser=0, missing seccomp, capabilities not dropped). That's admission control doing its job — the rogue workload never starts.

Now prove the network boundary from a compliant pod:

# a compliant (non-root, no caps) pod lands, but egress is denied except DNS + OTel
kubectl -n agent-sandbox run probe --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"probe","image":"curlimages/curl:8.10.1","securityContext":{"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":65534,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}},"command":["sleep","120"]}]}}' \
  --command -- sleep 120

kubectl -n agent-sandbox exec probe -- curl -s -m 5 https://example.com || echo "BLOCKED (expected)"
kubectl -n agent-sandbox delete pod probe rogue --ignore-not-found

The external curl times out → the default-deny egress policy is working.

Stronger isolation later

The baseline is PSA + NetworkPolicy, which needs no extra controller. For runtime-level isolation (gVisor/Kata-backed pods) you can layer on kagent substrate or kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox — both are additive and don't remove this baseline. See cluster/agent-sandbox/README.md.

docs.title: Part B — Tetragon (eBPF runtime security)
docs.text: Tetragon attaches eBPF programs to the kernel to observe — and optionally enforce — process execution and network behaviour, with almost no overhead. It was installed as a DaemonSet in module 01 (cluster/tetragon/).

docs.title: Verify Tetragon is running
docs.text: kubectl -n tetragon get pods            # tetragon DaemonSet + tetragon-operator Ready

docs.title: Watch what your agents actually do
docs.text:
Stream live process/network events with the tetra CLI that ships inside the DaemonSet pod. Leave this running in one terminal, then send a prompt to the SRE agent (module 02) in another:

kubectl -n tetragon exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact

You'll see a line for every process_exec and network connection across the node — including the processes the kagent agents spawn when they run a tool. This is your ground-truth audit log: what did the agent's container actually execute?

Filter to the interesting bits

tetra getevents -o compact --pods <pod> narrows the stream to a single pod. Pipe to grep for a specific binary (e.g. grep curl) to catch an agent reaching for the network.

docs.title: Optional: enforce, don't just observe
docs.text:
Tetragon can turn an observation into a kill. A TracingPolicy can, for example, Sigkill any process in the sandbox that tries to execute an unexpected binary. This is powerful but kernel-dependent on a shared Codespace host — see the troubleshooting note below before relying on enforcement.

# Illustrative — a policy that kills shells spawned inside the sandbox namespace.
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicyNamespaced
metadata:
  name: no-shell-in-sandbox
  namespace: agent-sandbox
spec:
  kprobes:
    - call: "sys_execve"
      syscall: true
      args:
        - index: 0
          type: "string"
      selectors:
        - matchArgs:
            - index: 0
              operator: "Postfix"
              values: ["/bin/sh", "/bin/bash"]
          matchActions:
            - action: Sigkill

eBPF on a Codespace kernel

k3d/kind nodes share the Codespace host kernel. Observation (getevents) works on most hosts; enforcement (Sigkill) may be unavailable on a restricted host kernel. If Tetragon pods CrashLoop, see Troubleshooting → Tetragon.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• The agent-sandbox namespace rejects privileged/root pods and blocks egress except DNS + telemetry.
  • Tetragon streams real exec/network events from your running agents, giving you a runtime audit trail (and an optional enforcement hook).

Your agents can now act — but only inside a box you drew, under a sensor that watches. Next: 04 — Observe with Dynatrace to see cost and performance of every agent run.

docs.title: 04 — Observe with Dynatrace AI Observability
docs.text:
You now have agents running (module 02) inside a secured sandbox (module 03). But are they fast? Reliable? How much are they costing you per run? This module uses Dynatrace AI Observability to answer that — turning the spans your agents already emit into cost, token, latency, and quality signals.

Nothing to install here

The pipeline was wired in module 01: kagent's otel.tracing sends every LLM call, tool call, and agent hop as an OTLP span to the gateway collector, which forwards to both Dynatrace and Phoenix. This module is about reading that data in Dynatrace.

docs.title: How agent telemetry reaches Dynatrace
docs.text:
kagent Agent (LLM + tool spans, gen_ai.* semconv)
        │ OTLP 4317
        ▼
 otel-gateway-collector ──▶ Dynatrace tenant (OTLP ingest)   ← you are here
   (normalises OpenInference/Traceloop → gen_ai.*)  └▶ Phoenix (module 06)

The gateway normalises OpenInference/Traceloop LLM attributes onto the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* semantic conventions, so Dynatrace sees consistent gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, and token/latency fields regardless of which instrumentation a tool used.

docs.title: 1. Generate some traffic
docs.text:
Observability needs something to observe. Send a few prompts so there are runs to inspect (from module 02):

# SRE agent — a couple of diagnostic prompts
kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List pods in all namespaces and summarise anything not Running."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/sre-agent

Run a BMAD workflow too if you want a longer, multi-hop trace to look at.

docs.title: 2. Open AI Observability in Dynatrace
docs.text:
In your Dynatrace tenant (the .apps.dynatrace.com URL from module 02), open AI Observability (apps menu → Observe & Explore → AI & LLM Observability, or search the app launcher for "AI Observability").

What you should see

A list of AI/LLM services and model endpoints. Because every agent shares the workshop-llm ModelConfig (DeepSeek), you'll see the DeepSeek endpoint with call volume, token usage, latency distribution, error rate, and an estimated cost per call and in aggregate.

docs.title: 3. The four questions to ask every agent run
docs.text:
Dynatrace AI Observability is organised around the metrics that drive the workshop's cost-efficiency theme. For each agent, look at:

Question Where to look What "good" looks like How much does a run cost? Token usage × model price → estimated cost per request / per service. Stable, proportional to task size — no silent blow-ups. Where does the latency go? Span waterfall: model time vs tool time vs agent-to-agent hops. Model/tool time dominates; little idle gap. Is it reliable? Error rate + failure spans (tool errors, model timeouts, A2A failures). Low, with clear error messages when it does fail. Is it efficient? Tokens per task, number of tool calls per task, retries. No redundant tool calls, no runaway token growth.

docs.title: 4. Follow a single trace end to end
docs.text:
Click into one agent request. The distributed trace shows the full loop:

 message/send (A2A)
 └─ agent.run                         (the whole loop)
    ├─ gen_ai LLM call  model=deepseek-chat  in=1.2k out=340 tokens  420ms
    ├─ tool: k8s.list_pods            180ms
    ├─ gen_ai LLM call  in=1.9k out=120 tokens  380ms
    └─ final answer

Each gen_ai span carries the model, the input/output token counts, and the latency — so you can see exactly which step spent the tokens. For a BMAD run, you additionally see the orchestrator's A2A hops to the analyst → PM → architect → developer → QA agents as nested spans.

Build a cost view with DQL

The Dynatrace MCP server (module 02) lets the SRE agent query this itself, but you can also open Notebooks and run DQL against the spans, e.g. sum gen_ai.usage.output_tokens grouped by agent to rank your most expensive agents. That ranking is the raw material for module 07 (Optimize).

docs.title: 5. Correlate with the rest of the cluster
docs.text: Because module 01 also installed the Dynatrace Operator in Kubernetes-monitoring mode, the agent traces sit next to your cluster topology. Under Kubernetes you can line up an expensive agent run against pod CPU/memory, restarts, and node pressure — so "slow agent" vs "starved pod" is one click apart.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• Every agent run appears in Dynatrace AI Observability with cost, tokens, latency, and error signals.
  • You can open a single trace and attribute spend to a specific model or tool call, and correlate it with Kubernetes health.

Next: 05 — Diagnose a broken cluster — stop sending toy prompts: inject a real failure and watch the SRE agent find the root cause.

docs.title: 05 — Diagnose a broken cluster with kagent
docs.text:
You have agents running (module 02), secured (module 03), and their every run flowing into Dynatrace as cost, token, latency, and quality signals (module 04). But so far nothing has broken. The sre-agent has only answered toy prompts ("list the pods"). This module is the payoff: inject a real Kubernetes failure, ask the agent, and watch it reach the root cause — then grade its answer against a ground-truth key.

Nothing new to install

This module reuses the module-02 sre-agent exactly as-is. It already has the right surface — read/investigate tools (k8s_get_resources, k8s_describe_resource, k8s_get_pod_logs, k8s_get_events), a minimal non-destructive operate set (scale/patch/rollout), and the full Dynatrace MCP — and a system prompt that is a "Findings → Root cause → Action → Verify" SRE loop. Nothing here grants the agent new destructive power; there is no k8s_delete_resource.

docs.title: Why break things
docs.text:
You can't convince yourself an AI agent can do first-line SRE triage by watching it on a healthy cluster. You validate it the way a real on-call does: break something you understand, ask the agent, and check its answer against what you know is wrong. That is the diagnosis loop the scenarios/ directory encodes:

 run.sh inject <id>   ──▶   a real, isolated fault lands in workshop-faults
          │
          ▼
 paste <id>/prompt.md into the sre-agent (kagent UI or A2A curl)
          │
          ▼
 agent gathers evidence  →  Findings → Root cause → Action → Verify
          │
          ▼
 grade the answer against <id>/expected-diagnosis.md  (objective key)
          │
          ▼
 run.sh cleanup <id>  ──▶   fault removed, zero residue

Each scenario ships three files: manifests.yaml (the breakage), prompt.md (the exact prompt to paste — it never names the root cause), and expected-diagnosis.md (the objective answer key). The infra scenarios sit on distinct evidence channels on purpose — logs vs. events vs. terminated-reason — so even a small model (DeepSeek-V3) can be graded without ambiguity.

docs.title: Prereqs
docs.text:
• SRE agent deployed — module 02 (sre-agent in the kagent namespace). This is the only hard requirement for scenarios 01–03.
  • (Scenario 12 only) Observe pipeline live — module 04, plus the opt-in opentelemetry-demo-light app. Scenario 12 is the Dynatrace-correlation scenario and is skippable (see the callout below).

Scenario 12 has an extra resource footprint — skippable on the minimum tier

Scenarios 01–03 are self-contained and cost almost nothing: each spins up one throwaway Deployment. Scenario 12 additionally needs the opt-in opentelemetry-demo-light astronomy-shop app deployed (and Dynatrace, to show the correlation). On a minimum 4-core / 16 GB Codespace, skip 12 and run 01–03 — you still get the full infra-diagnosis payoff. Only enable 12 if you have headroom: 

INSTALL_OTEL_DEMO=true bash cluster/install.sh   # one-time, opt-in (module 01 / ISI-6847)
If otel-demo is not deployed, run.sh inject 12 fails fast and prints this exact command — nothing breaks, you're just told cleanly why 12 is unavailable.

List what's available any time:

bash scenarios/run.sh list     # id, title, and an [app-dep: otel-demo] tag on #12

docs.title: Walkthrough — scenario 01, CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text: The rest of this page walks the canonical "hello world" of k8s diagnosis end to end. Scenarios 02 (ImagePullBackOff) and 03 (OOMKilled) follow the exact same four steps — just swap the id and paste that scenario's prompt.md.

docs.title: 1. Inject the fault
docs.text:
bash scenarios/run.sh inject 01-crashloopbackoff   # id can be '01' or the full name

run.sh creates the dedicated workshop-faults namespace and applies the fault's manifests.yaml. A fail-closed allowlist rejects any manifest that references kagent, dynatrace, the module-03 agent-sandbox, or any platform namespace before anything is applied — the blast radius is one throwaway namespace. Watch it break:

kubectl get pods -n workshop-faults

NAME                              READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
billing-worker-5c9f8d7b6c-ab12x   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4          90s

docs.title: 2. Ask the agent
docs.text:
Open each scenario's prompt.md and paste the prompt exactly — it describes the symptom and asks for evidence, but it never tells the agent the root cause. For scenario 01 (scenarios/01-crashloopbackoff/prompt.md):

kagent UIA2A (curl)

Open the kagent UI (http://localhost:8080), pick sre-agent, and paste:

A pod in the workshop-faults namespace keeps restarting. Investigate what is wrong with the workload there, find the root cause, and tell me the exact evidence (status, events, and logs) that supports it.

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"A pod in the workshop-faults namespace keeps restarting. Investigate the workload there, find the root cause, and cite the exact status, events, and log lines that support it."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/sre-agent

The agent will walk its SRE loop live: list the pods, describe the failing one, pull its events and logs, and converge on a conclusion.

docs.title: 3. Grade it
docs.text:
Open the scenario's expected-diagnosis.md — the objective answer key — and check the agent's conclusion against it. Scenario 01's key wants the agent to:

  • report billing-worker in CrashLoopBackOff;
  • cite the non-zero exit code (1) from lastState.terminated;
  • quote the Back-off restarting failed container event;
  • quote the fatal log line (BILLING_DB_URL is not set);
  • conclude the start command fails on launch.

The key also lists a pass_threshold (how many signals must be cited) and a Must NOT claim section that catches small-model confabulation — e.g. for the crash-loop, claiming an ImagePullBackOff (scenario 02) or OOMKilled (scenario 03) is an unambiguous fail, because those are different evidence channels. That cross-channel discipline is why the diagnosis is graded objectively.

Each infra scenario exercises a different sense

01 reads logs, 02 reads events (Failed to pull image — no logs exist yet, so a logs-only agent is stuck), and 03 reads lastState.terminated.reason: OOMKilled (it looks like a crash loop until you check why it was killed). Running all three proves the agent reads the right signal for each failure class, not just one trick.

docs.title: 4. (Optional) Remediate & verify
docs.text:
Ask the agent for the minimal safe fix, then watch it act within its non-destructive operate set:

You found the root cause. Propose and apply the minimal, safe fix, then verify the pod reaches a healthy state.

For scenario 01 that means supplying the missing configuration (or correcting the start command) and rolling out the Deployment — k8s_patch_resource + k8s_rollout, never a delete. Re-run kubectl get pods -n workshop-faults and confirm the pod goes Running. The agent can only patch/apply/scale/rollout, so this stays safe by construction.

docs.title: 5. Cleanup
docs.text:
bash scenarios/run.sh cleanup 01-crashloopbackoff   # deletes the workshop-faults ns — zero residue

Cleanup is one command and idempotent. For infra scenarios it deletes exactly the workshop-faults namespace; it never touches kagent, dynatrace, the demo app, or any platform namespace.

docs.title: The Dynatrace money shot — scenario 12 (optional)
docs.text:
Scenarios 01–03 are diagnosable from cluster state alone. Scenario 12 is the one that shows off the workshop's real differentiator: the agent correlating Kubernetes with Dynatrace. A faulty product-catalog backend joins the product-catalog Service's endpoints, so a fraction of the astronomy shop's product requests are load-balanced to it and fail — intermittent 5xx, not a clean outage.

bash scenarios/run.sh inject 12      # adds a faulty product-catalog backend (via inject.sh)

Paste scenarios/12-intermittent-5xx/prompt.md and point the agent at Dynatrace:

Users of the astronomy shop (namespace otel-demo) are seeing intermittent errors when they browse products — some requests work, some fail. Use Dynatrace to find the open problem and its Davis root cause, correlate it with the cluster state, and tell me which service is actually at fault and why.

A correct answer cites an open Dynatrace problem on the product path, names product-catalog as the Davis root-cause entity (not the frontend that merely surfaces it), notes the failures are intermittent (a partial error rate), and corroborates with k8s that the product-catalog Service has an extra, unhealthy backend in rotation. Grade against its expected-diagnosis.md (pass_threshold: 4). Clean up with:

bash scenarios/run.sh cleanup 12     # removes only the faulty backend — never the healthy demo

docs.title: So what — these runs feed the rest of the workshop
docs.text:
This module isn't a detour; it's the fuel for everything after it.

Every diagnosis run you just made is reusable evidence

  • Eval fixtures for 06 — Evaluate: each expected-diagnosis.md doubles as ground truth — the same Required signals / Must NOT claim keys become the scoring rubric for Phoenix and dt-evals. You now have real, labelled traces to grade, not toy prompts.
  • Cost data for 07 — Optimize: every run emitted gen_ai.* spans with token, cost, and latency. A diagnosis is a realistic, multi-tool task — exactly the kind of run whose token spend module 07 teaches you to cut without losing accuracy.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• You injected a real, isolated Kubernetes fault and the module-02 sre-agent reached the correct root cause, citing the exact signals.
  • You graded its answer objectively against expected-diagnosis.md, and (optionally) watched it remediate within its non-destructive tool set.
  • Cleanup left zero residue — the platform and module-03 isolation boundary were never touched.

Next: 06 — Evaluate (Phoenix + dt-evals) — you diagnosed and graded by hand here; now turn those answer keys into an automated eval suite.

docs.title: 06 — Evaluate (Phoenix + dt-evals)
docs.text:
Observability (module 04) tells you what the agent did and what it cost. It does not tell you whether the answer was correct, grounded, or useful. That's evaluation — scoring agent outputs against expectations — and it's the step most teams skip, which is why their agents quietly regress.

Both tools here evaluate the same gen_ai.* spans the OTel gateway already produces (module 02/04) — you don't re-run the agents to grade them, you grade the traces they already emitted:

  • Phoenix (Arize) — interactive trace + eval UI, already running from module 01. Great for exploratory LLM-as-a-judge over live traces.
  • dt-evals — dynatrace-oss/dt-evals, the primary path: a config-driven CLI that pulls gen_ai.* spans from Dynatrace, scores them with a judge, and writes the results back as bizevents next to the rest of your telemetry.

Everything for this module lives under evals/. Both paths reuse the cost-efficient workshop judge — DeepSeek (deepseek-chat), the same model that powers the agents — set once in evals/.env (copy from evals/.env.example).

Generate traffic first

Evals score real traces. Drive the SRE agent or a BMAD task (module 02) before running either path, so there are spans to grade.

docs.title: Part A — Phoenix: explore and judge live traces
docs.text:
Open Phoenix on the forwarded Codespace port 6006:

kubectl -n phoenix port-forward svc/phoenix 6006:6006
# then open http://localhost:6006

Every agent run shows up as an LLM trace: prompt, response, tool spans, token counts. Click a span to see its gen_ai.* attributes.

docs.title: Run an evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge)
docs.text:
The repo ships a small, version-pinned eval script that builds two judge classifiers — hallucination (is the answer grounded in its context?) and relevance (does it answer the question?):

cd evals && uv sync
# Bundled sample dataset — no cluster/traffic needed (just a judge key):
uv run python phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py
# Live spans pulled from Phoenix, scores logged back onto the traces:
uv run python phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py --from-phoenix

It prints a per-metric summary, writes phoenix/out/phoenix_eval_results.csv, and (with --from-phoenix) annotates the originating spans so the labels show up on the traces in the UI. Details: evals/phoenix/README.md.

This is exploratory: fast, visual, good for discovering failure modes. For a gate you can run in CI, use dt-evals.

docs.title: Part B — dt-evals: trace-sourced evals in Dynatrace
docs.text:
dt-evals is the primary eval path. It samples gen_ai.* spans from your Dynatrace environment, masks PII, scores each with an LLM judge, and writes gen_ai.evaluation.result bizevents back — so a low score is one click from the trace, prompt, and tool calls that caused it.

Dynatrace gen_ai.* spans ─► dt-evals (sample → mask → judge) ─► bizevents ─► DQL / dashboard / alert

docs.title: 1. Credentials
docs.text:
dt-evals needs (put these in evals/.env). You created these during onboarding — see Start the benchmark → Create the required tokens for exact scopes and where each is generated:

Var What DYNATRACE_API_TOKEN a dedicated dt0c01 token with storage:spans:read + storage:events:write (not the Phase-2 OTLP token) — token C DT_ENVIRONMENT_URL your …apps.dynatrace.com URL (derived from DT_TENANT_URL if unset) OPENAI_API_KEY judge key — a DeepSeek key works (token D) DT_EVAL_SERVICE the agent's service.name — discover it, don't guess

Discover the service with DQL (Dynatrace Notebook):

fetch spans, from: now() - 2h
| filter isNotNull(gen_ai.operation.name) or isNotNull(gen_ai.request.model)
| summarize span_count = count(), by: { service.name }
| sort span_count desc

docs.title: 2. Run it
docs.text:
The CLI runs via npx (Node ≥ 22); the wrapper renders the config (evals/dt-evals/workshop-agents.dt-eval.yaml) with your env values and runs validate + run:

cd evals/dt-evals
./run-dt-eval.sh

The config enables agent-relevant metrics (relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, coherence, toxicity, prompt-injection) and sets alert thresholds that make the run exit non-zero on a breach — a ready-made CI gate.

docs.title: 3. Read the scores
docs.text:
fetch bizevents
| filter event.type == "gen_ai.evaluation.result"
| summarize avg(toDouble(gen_ai.evaluation.score.value)), by: { gen_ai.evaluation.name }

Shared vs per-attendee tenant

dt-evals reads spans and writes bizevents scoped by service.name. The workshop default is a per-attendee Dynatrace tenant (a free trial is enough) so nobody grades anyone else's traffic; a shared-tenant fallback with per-attendee service.name suffixes is documented in evals/dt-evals/README.md.

docs.title: Part C — grade a diagnosis against the answer key
docs.text:
Parts A/B judge generic quality (grounded? relevant? toxic?). The diagnostic module (05 — Diagnose) asks a sharper question: when the SRE agent investigates a real injected fault, did it reach the right root cause? Each scenario ships an objective answer key — scenarios/<id>/expected-diagnosis.md — and those keys are registered as this module's diagnosis-grading ground truth under evals/ground-truth/.

The grading check:

Did the diagnosis cite ≥ pass_threshold of the answer key's required signals (root cause + evidence channel), identify the root cause, and avoid the forbidden cross-channel claims?

Because scenarios 01–03 sit on distinct evidence channels (logs vs. events vs. OOMKilled status), a cross-channel claim is an unambiguous fail — so this grades objectively, even with no judge model.

docs.title: Deterministic grade (offline, no key)
docs.text:
cd evals
python phoenix/run_diagnosis_eval.py        # bundled golden + confab diagnoses

It prints a PASS/FAIL per diagnosis and writes phoenix/out/diagnosis_eval_results.csv. Add --llm-judge (needs a judge key) to also run an LLM root-cause grader, or --from-phoenix to grade the agent's live diagnosis spans and annotate them back onto the traces.

docs.title: In Dynatrace (dt-evals)
docs.text:
Each answer key is also rendered into a dt-evals custom evaluator. Register the one for the scenario you ran, then grade its spans:

cd evals/dt-evals
npx -y "$DT_EVALS_PKG" evaluators add            # paste evaluators/diagnosis-<id>.md
./run-dt-eval.sh --config scenario-diagnosis.dt-eval.yaml --metric diagnosis-<id>

Correct diagnoses score 1, misses score 0 — a per-scenario pass/fail bizevent next to the trace. Details: evals/ground-truth/README.md.

Closing the diagnose → evaluate → optimize loop

The same diagnosis runs you grade here emit the gen_ai.* spans whose token/cost/latency drive 07 — Optimize. Break it (05 — Diagnose), grade it (06), cut the waste (07).

docs.title: What to measure for these agents
docs.text: Agent Good eval questions SRE agent Did it correctly identify the unhealthy pod? Did it call the right k8s/Dynatrace tool (not guess)? Was the diagnosis grounded in real tool output (no hallucinated pod names)? BMAD crew Did the workflow produce the expected artifacts (issues → branch → PR)? Did the developer agent stay within its repo scope? Did it finish within a token budget?

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• A Phoenix eval run produces labelled scores you can inspect in the UI (or the CSV) — even offline against the bundled dataset.
  • A dt-evals run scores the agents' real traces and lands the results in Dynatrace as queryable bizevents, with a CI-friendly pass/fail gate.
  • A diagnosis-grading run (Part C) scores an SRE-agent diagnosis against a scenario answer key — PASS/FAIL against registered ground truth, offline or in Dynatrace.

Next: 07 — Optimize — now that you can measure cost and quality, go cut the waste.

docs.title: 07 — Optimize
docs.text:
This is where the whole workshop pays off. You can now run agents (02), secure them (03), observe their cost (04), and evaluate their quality (05). Optimization is the loop that uses that evidence to make agents cheaper without making them worse.

The core idea

The biggest driver of AI agent cost is tokens — and most token spend is waste: unused tools inflating every prompt, oversized system prompts, chatty multi-hop workflows, and retries. You can't cut what you can't see, which is why observation and evaluation came first.

docs.title: The optimization loop
docs.text:
observe (04)        evaluate (05)
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
   find the waste  ──▶  make one change  ──▶  re-measure cost + quality
       ▲                                            │
       └────────────── keep only if quality holds ──┘

Change one thing, re-run the eval suite, and keep the change only if quality holds and cost dropped. Never optimize on cost alone — that's how you ship a cheap agent that gives wrong answers.

Two ready-made surfaces — deploy them first

This module ships a Dynatrace dashboard and notebook that compute every signal below from your crew's gen_ai.* spans. Deploy them, then read the rest of this page with your own data on screen:

dtctl config use-context <your-tenant>
cd cluster/dynatrace/optimization
dtctl apply -f ai-agent-optimization.dashboard.yaml
dtctl create notebook -f ai-agent-optimization-before-after.notebook.yaml
  • Dashboard — AI Agent Optimization: spend ranking, input:output ratio, tools-actually-used, loop detection, token-trend.
  • Notebook — AI Agent Optimization — before/after: the observe → find → change → re-measure → keep/revert walkthrough, one runnable DQL cell per step.

All four artifacts (dashboard, notebook, guardian, workflow — §4) are dtctl-ready YAML in cluster/dynatrace/optimization/ with a README.

docs.title: 1. Rank your agents by spend
docs.text:
From Dynatrace AI Observability (module 04), find your most expensive agents — total tokens and estimated cost per run. Start at the top of that list; a 20% cut on your priciest agent beats a 50% cut on a rarely-used one.

fetch spans
| filter service.namespace == "kagent" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(),
    inputTokens  = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens),
    outputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens),
    by:{agent = service.name}
| fieldsAdd totalTokens = inputTokens + outputTokens,
    inOutRatio      = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / outputTokens, decimals: 1),
    avgInputPerCall = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / llmCalls)
| sort totalTokens desc

What this looked like on the reference tenant (7-day window)

Agent Total tokens in:out ratio Avg input / call seta_sre_investigator 46.2 M 38 : 1 33,180 bmad_orchestrator 11.8 M 14 : 1 8,762 bmad_developer 2.7 M 3 : 1 6,191

The whole crew burned 64 M tokens, and one agent — the SRE investigator — is 72% of it. Note the input : output ratio: 38 input tokens for every output token means the model re-reads a large context on every call. That ratio, not the raw total, is your waste compass. Start there.

docs.title: a) Remove tools the agent never uses
docs.text:
Every tool an agent is granted is described in every prompt sent to the model — that's input tokens on every single call, whether the tool is used or not. In the traces, look at which tools an agent actually calls over many runs; anything never called is pure overhead.

Trim the agent's toolNames to only what it uses:

# agents/sre/sre-agent.yaml (illustrative)
spec:
  tools:
    - type: McpServer
      mcpServer:
        toolNames:        # ← keep only the tools this agent actually calls
          - list_pods
          - get_logs
          - dql_query
          # dropped: a dozen k8s tools the SRE agent never invoked

List the tools the agent actually calls straight from the traces, then diff against its granted set:

fetch spans
| filter service.namespace == "kagent" and service.name == "seta_sre_investigator"
    and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool" and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"
| summarize calls = count(), by:{tool = gen_ai.tool.name}
| sort calls desc

Measure the schema tax directly

Each tool is a JSON schema injected into every prompt. On the reference tenant one captured call_llm request carried 7 tool declarations costing ~1,160 input tokens — about 165 tokens per tool, on every call. The shipped SRE agent (agents/sre/sre-agent.yaml) attaches the Dynatrace MCP server with no toolNames filter (every discovered tool) plus 15 k8s tools. Pin toolNames to the handful the traces prove it uses and you reclaim those tokens on all 1,357 calls — before touching anything else.

Re-apply (bash agents/install-agents.sh), send the same prompts, and compare input-token counts in Dynatrace. Fewer tools → smaller prompts → lower cost on every call.

docs.title: b) Tighten the system prompt
docs.text: A rambling system prompt is a fixed tax on every request. Shorten it to the essentials; move examples out unless they measurably improve the eval score.

docs.title: c) Fix chatty workflows
docs.text:
In a BMAD run, the span waterfall (module 04) shows how many A2A hops and LLM calls a task took. Redundant hand-offs, an agent that re-reads context it already has, or a loop that retries silently all show up as extra gen_ai spans. Collapse the hops that don't earn their tokens.

fetch spans
| filter service.namespace == "kagent" and span.name == "call_llm"
| summarize llmCalls = count(), inputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens),
    by:{agent = service.name, task = gen_ai.task.id}
| filter llmCalls >= 5
| sort inputTokens desc

Loops are where big agents actually bleed

On the reference tenant the SRE investigator's heaviest task made 7 call_llm hops and re-sent 228,000 input tokens — the same growing context pushed to the model again and again. For an already-lean agent (few tools, tight prompt) this loop re-send, not unused tools, is the dominant cost. The dashboard's loop table ranks these so you fix the worst first.

docs.title: d) Right-size the model per agent
docs.text:
Not every agent needs the most capable model. kagent makes the model a one-line ModelConfig reference, so you can point a cheap, mechanical agent (e.g. a formatter) at a smaller/cheaper model while the reasoning-heavy orchestrator keeps the stronger one. This workshop already defaults the whole crew to DeepSeek for cost; per-agent tuning goes further.

# agents/mcp/00-modelconfig.yaml — the shared workshop-llm (DeepSeek, cost-first)
# Create a second, cheaper ModelConfig and reference it from the agents that
# don't need the strong model. One field per agent: spec.modelConfig.

docs.title: 3. Prove the win
docs.text:
Open the before/after notebook (deployed above). Its §5 cell measures the one number that moves — average input tokens per call_llm — and the section time-picker is how you switch the before and after windows:

fetch spans
| filter service.namespace == "kagent" and service.name == "seta_sre_investigator"
    and span.name == "call_llm" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(),
    avgInputPerCall    = round(avg(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)),
    medianInputPerCall = round(median(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)),
    totalInputTokens   = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens)

The procedure, in order:

  1. Run the query over a window before the change — record avgInputPerCall.
  2. Make one change (trim tools / tighten prompt / collapse hops / right-size model).
  3. Re-apply and replay the same prompts.
  4. Run the query over the after window and run the dt-evals suite (module 06).

Fill the scorecard from those two runs:

Metric Before After Keep? Avg input tokens / call (§5 notebook) (§5 notebook) — Est. cost / task — — — Eval pass rate (module 06) (module 06) ✅ only if ≥ before

The rule

Ship the change when cost went down and the eval pass rate did not. If quality dropped, revert — the cheaper agent that's wrong is more expensive than the costly one that's right.

docs.title: 4. Make it continuous — the guardian + workflow
docs.text:
Optimization isn't a one-off. Because cost and quality are now both telemetry, the workshop ships two more dtctl-ready artifacts in cluster/dynatrace/optimization/ that turn the optimization loop into an automated gate:

A Site Reliability Guardian (ai-agent-quality-cost.guardian.yaml) — three DQL objectives over the crew's call_llm spans, so a regression fails loudly:

Objective SLI Rule target / warning Cost per LLM call avg input tokens / call ≤ 20,000 / 18,000 Loop efficiency avg hops / task ≤ 5 / 4 Answer substance (quality proxy) avg output tokens / call ≥ 200 / 300 
dtctl create settings -f ai-agent-quality-cost.guardian.yaml \
  --schema app:dynatrace.site.reliability.guardian:guardians --scope environment

The quality proxy backstops the cost cuts — an agent that got "cheaper" by emitting truncated answers trips it. For the full LLM-judge quality gate, pair the guardian with the Phase-4 dt-evals suite (module 06).

A scheduled Workflow (ai-agent-optimization.workflow.yaml) runs that guardian daily over the last 24h (schedule ships disabled — flip trigger.schedule.isActive: true to go continuous):

dtctl create workflow -f ai-agent-optimization.workflow.yaml

Beyond the guardian:

  • Keep the dt-evals suite in CI as a regression + budget gate on every agent change.
  • Watch the dashboard's token-trend tile; the guardian alerts when an agent's tokens-per-call drifts up.
  • Re-rank your agents periodically — usage patterns change, and today's cheap agent is tomorrow's top spender.

docs.title: What you achieved (acceptance)
docs.text:
• You identified the most expensive agents from real telemetry.
  • You applied at least one concrete cut (unused tools / prompt / hops / model) and proved with evals that quality held while cost fell.
  • You have a repeatable loop — observe → evaluate → change → re-measure — to keep agents cost-efficient in production.

docs.title: You've completed the arc
docs.text:
Why → kagent → cluster → agents → secure → observe → evaluate → optimize. You built a full, cost-efficient AI-agent platform on Kubernetes and have the telemetry and evals to keep it that way.

Stuck on anything? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: kagent in 5 minutes
docs.text: Before you build anything, here's the mental model for kagent — the piece that turns "an LLM calling some tools" into agents you can deploy, secure, observe, and evaluate like any other Kubernetes workload.

docs.title: Why run agents on Kubernetes at all?
docs.text:
An AI agent is a loop: a model reads a goal, decides which tool to call, reads the result, and repeats until it's done. Run that loop from a laptop script and you get no isolation, no shared credentials story, no telemetry, and no way for one agent to hand work to another. kagent moves the loop onto Kubernetes, so an agent becomes a first-class, declarative object — reconciled by a controller, scheduled onto nodes, and wired into the same observability and security tooling as the rest of your platform.

The one-line definition

kagent is an agentic runtime for Kubernetes. You describe agents, models, and tools as custom resources; a controller runs them, exposes them over a standard agent-to-agent (A2A) API, and keeps them reconciled.

docs.title: The four objects you'll meet
docs.text:
kagent ships a handful of CRDs. In this workshop you only need four of them:

CRD What it is Where you'll see it ModelConfig Which LLM an agent talks to (provider, model, endpoint, secret). agents/mcp/00-modelconfig.yaml — the shared workshop-llm (DeepSeek). Agent A deployed agent: a system prompt + a ModelConfig + the tools it may call. the SRE agent and the six BMAD agents (module 02). MCPServer A tool server that runs inside the cluster (stdio or HTTP). GitHub MCP (module 02). RemoteMCPServer A reference to a tool server reached over the network, whose tools kagent discovers. the built-in kagent-tool-server, Dynatrace MCP (module 02).

Everything else — the controller, the UI, the bundled database, and kmcp (the MCP plumbing) — runs for you once the platform is installed (module 01).

docs.title: How a tool call actually happens
docs.text:
you ──prompt──▶  Agent (loop)
                    │  "I need to list pods"
                    ▼
              ModelConfig ──▶ LLM picks a tool + arguments
                    │
                    ▼
            MCP tool server (kagent-tool-server / github / dynatrace)
                    │  returns a result
                    ▼
              Agent feeds result back to the LLM ──▶ repeat ──▶ final answer

Two acronyms matter:

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard for how an agent discovers and calls tools. kagent speaks it, so any MCP server — GitHub's, Dynatrace's, or your own — plugs in the same way.
  • A2A (Agent-to-Agent) is the protocol agents use to call each other. The BMAD orchestrator delegates to the analyst, PM, architect, developer, and QA agents over A2A; that's how a "crew" works when there is no Team CRD.

docs.title: Why it fits this workshop's theme
docs.text:
The whole lab is about cost-efficient agents. Because kagent makes each tool call, model call, and agent hand-off a real span emitted over OpenTelemetry (we wire this in module 01), you can see where tokens and latency actually go — and in module 07 you use that evidence to cut the waste. No runtime, no visibility; no visibility, no optimization.

You don't configure kagent by hand here

Every object above is applied for you by the scripts in modules 01–02. This page is just so the YAML you're about to read makes sense. If you want the full CRD reference, see the kagent docs.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Head to 00 — Setup (Codespace) to boot the environment, then install the platform in module 01.

docs.title: Run of show — the guided 13-step demo
docs.text:
This page is the single, top-to-bottom script for the live demo. It stitches the workshop's modules into one continuous run: configure an agent, investigate a cluster, turn on observability, evaluate the results, and close the observe → evaluate → optimize loop. Each step is deliberately short — just enough to do it — and links to the full module when you want the depth behind it.

How to read this page

Every step has the same shape: What & why (one line), Do it (the exact commands), Apply this (the config or prompt to paste), and Go deeper (the module link). Run the steps in order — later steps depend on the traffic and traces the earlier ones produce.

Prerequisites

The cluster is up and the platform is installed — that's 00 — Setup and 01 — Platform install. After those, the OpenTelemetry Operator, a gateway collector, kagent (clean base, no agents yet), Tetragon, and Phoenix are all running. This walkthrough starts from there.

Two surfaces to keep open

Forward the two UIs once, in a spare terminal, and leave them up for the whole run: 

kubectl -n kagent  port-forward svc/kagent-ui 8080:8080 &   # kagent UI  → http://localhost:8080
kubectl -n phoenix port-forward svc/phoenix   6006:6006 &   # Phoenix    → http://localhost:6006
Dynatrace is your tenant's …apps.dynatrace.com URL (from module 02).

docs.title: Step 1 — Configure kagent to create an agent
docs.text:
What & why. kagent shipped as a clean runtime in module 01. Here you turn on its built-in Kubernetes tooling, point it at a model, wire the pre-deployed MCP servers, and deploy the SRE agent — one idempotent script does all of it.

Do it. Supply the MCP credentials, then install:

export GH_PAT='github_pat_...'                              # fine-grained, one demo repo
export DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN='dt0s16....'                       # Dynatrace platform token
export DT_ENVIRONMENT='https://<env>.apps.dynatrace.com'    # platform apps URL

bash agents/install-agents.sh

The script applies, in order: the MCP layer (the shared workshop-llm ModelConfig — DeepSeek — plus the GitHub and Dynatrace MCP tool servers), then the SRE agent, then the BMAD crew. kagent's built-in kagent-tool-server (Kubernetes + networking tools) is already enabled in cluster/kagent/values.yaml.

Apply this. Confirm the tools registered and the agent is Accepted:

kubectl -n kagent get mcpserver,remotemcpserver
kubectl -n kagent get remotemcpserver kagent-tool-server -o jsonpath='{.status.discoveredTools[*].name}'; echo
kubectl -n kagent get agents          # sre-agent + six bmad-* should be Accepted

Go deeper. 02 — Agents & MCP wiring.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run a simple cluster investigation (SRE agent)
docs.text:
What & why. Prove the agent is alive and can reach its Kubernetes tools with a harmless read-only prompt. This is the "list the pods" baseline — no fault yet.

Do it. Paste the prompt into the sre-agent in the kagent UI (http://localhost:8080), or send it over A2A:

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List the pods in the kagent namespace and tell me if any are unhealthy."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/sre-agent

Apply this. You should get a grounded answer naming real pods — the agent called k8s_get_resources, it did not guess. Keep this first run; you'll compare its trace against the re-run in Step 4.

Go deeper. 02 — Agents & MCP wiring.

docs.title: Step 3 — Show the observability configuration in the collector
docs.text:
What & why. Every answer the agent just gave already emitted spans. The gateway collector is what turns those raw LLM/tool spans into clean, Dynatrace- and Phoenix-ready telemetry — and fans them out to both backends. Open its config so the audience sees there is no magic: it's a normalise + fan-out pipeline.

Do it. Show the live collector and its config:

kubectl get otelcol -n opentelemetry-operator-system          # the gateway collector

Open cluster/otel/collector-gateway.yaml and point at the two things that matter:

processors:
  # Normalise OpenInference / Traceloop LLM attributes onto gen_ai.* semconv
  transform/genai-normalize:
    trace_statements:
      - context: span
        statements:
          - set(attributes["gen_ai.usage.input_tokens"],  attributes["llm.token_count.prompt"])     where ...
          - set(attributes["gen_ai.usage.output_tokens"], attributes["llm.token_count.completion"])  where ...
          - set(attributes["gen_ai.request.model"],       attributes["llm.model_name"])              where ...
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, resourcedetection, resource, transform/genai-normalize, batch]
      exporters:  [otlphttp/dynatrace, otlp/phoenix, debug]   # ← fan-out to BOTH backends

Apply this. The takeaway for the room: whatever instrumentation a tool used (OpenInference, Traceloop, native OTel), the collector rewrites it onto the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* convention — so Dynatrace and Phoenix see the same model, token, and latency fields. The traces pipeline exports to Dynatrace and Phoenix from one place.

Go deeper. 04 — Observe with Dynatrace.

docs.title: Step 4 — Re-run the SRE investigation
docs.text:
What & why. Now that everyone has seen the pipeline, run the agent again — this time to generate traces on purpose. Same agent, slightly broader prompt, so there are fresh runs to open in Phoenix and Dynatrace in the next steps.

Do it.

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"List pods in all namespaces and summarise anything not Running."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/sre-agent

Apply this. Within a few seconds this run is a trace in both backends: an agent.run span wrapping gen_ai LLM calls and k8s tool calls, each carrying input/output token counts and latency. That trace is what Steps 5 and 6 inspect.

Go deeper. 04 — Observe with Dynatrace.

docs.title: Step 5 — Open Phoenix and create one evaluation
docs.text:
What & why. Observability shows what the agent did; evaluation scores whether it was any good. Phoenix is the fast, visual, exploratory judge — open it and run one LLM-as-a-judge evaluation over the traces you just made.

Do it. Phoenix is already forwarded on port 6006. Run the bundled eval:

cd evals && uv sync
uv run python phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py                # bundled sample dataset — just needs a judge key
uv run python phoenix/run_phoenix_eval.py --from-phoenix # grade the LIVE spans and annotate them in the UI

Apply this. The script builds two judge classifiers — hallucination (is the answer grounded in its context?) and relevance (does it answer the question?). With --from-phoenix it writes the scores back onto the originating spans, so the labels appear on the traces in the Phoenix UI. It also drops a CSV at evals/phoenix/out/phoenix_eval_results.csv.

Go deeper. 06 — Evaluate · Part A (Phoenix).

docs.title: Step 6 — Open Dynatrace: traces + AI Observability
docs.text:
What & why. Same spans, production-grade backend. Dynatrace adds estimated cost, a full distributed-trace waterfall, and correlation with cluster health — the signals that drive the workshop's cost-efficiency theme.

Do it. In your tenant (…apps.dynatrace.com), open the app launcher and go to AI & LLM Observability.

Apply this. Walk the four questions on one agent, then open a single trace:

Question Where to look How much does a run cost? token usage × model price → estimated cost per request Where does the latency go? span waterfall: model time vs tool time vs A2A hops Is it reliable? error rate + failure spans Is it efficient? tokens per task, tool calls per task, retries

Because every agent shares the workshop-llm (DeepSeek) ModelConfig, you'll see one DeepSeek endpoint with call volume, tokens, latency, error rate, and cost. Click into a request to see gen_ai LLM spans and k8s tool spans nested under agent.run.

Go deeper. 04 — Observe with Dynatrace.

docs.title: Step 7 — Create an evaluation using dt-evals
docs.text:
What & why. Phoenix was exploratory; dt-evals is the CI-friendly path. It samples gen_ai.* spans straight from Dynatrace, masks PII, scores each with a judge, and writes the results back as bizevents next to the rest of your telemetry — so a low score is one click from the trace that caused it.

Do it. Put the credentials in evals/.env, then run the wrapper:

cd evals/dt-evals
./run-dt-eval.sh          # renders the config with your env, then runs validate + run

The .env needs a dedicated DYNATRACE_API_TOKEN (dt0c01 with storage:spans:read + storage:events:write), DT_ENVIRONMENT_URL, a judge OPENAI_API_KEY (a DeepSeek key works), and DT_EVAL_SERVICE — discover that service name with DQL, don't guess it:

fetch spans, from: now() - 2h
| filter isNotNull(gen_ai.operation.name) or isNotNull(gen_ai.request.model)
| summarize span_count = count(), by: { service.name }
| sort span_count desc

Apply this. The shipped config enables relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, coherence, toxicity, and prompt-injection metrics, and sets thresholds that make the run exit non-zero on a breach — a ready-made CI gate.

Go deeper. 06 — Evaluate · Part B (dt-evals).

docs.title: Step 8 — Run the BMAD investigation
docs.text:
What & why. So far it's been the single SRE agent. Now show the other side of the platform: the BMAD crew — a six-member orchestrated workflow (analyst → PM → architect → developer → QA, driven by the orchestrator). A BMAD run is a long, multi-hop trace — exactly the kind of workload the optimize steps later target.

Do it. Send the orchestrator a task (kagent UI → bmad-orchestrator, or A2A):

kubectl run a2a --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -n kagent \
  --command -- curl -s -m 300 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"role":"user","messageId":"m1","kind":"message","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Build a simple Todo app in <owner>/<repo>. Run the full BMAD workflow and open a PR."}]}}}' \
  http://kagent-controller.kagent:8083/api/a2a/kagent/bmad-orchestrator

Apply this. In the trace you'll see the orchestrator's A2A hops to each crew member as nested spans, and the developer agent using the GitHub MCP tools to open issues, push a branch, and raise a PR. This is the multi-agent run whose hop-count and token spend you'll scrutinise in Step 12.

Go deeper. 02 — Agents & MCP wiring.

docs.title: Step 9 — Review the Phoenix evaluation
docs.text:
What & why. Close the loop you opened in Step 5: read the scores. Phoenix is where you discover failure modes interactively.

Do it. In the Phoenix UI (http://localhost:6006), open the traces you graded. Each now carries hallucination and relevance labels (from the --from-phoenix run). Sort by score to surface the weakest answers, and open one to read the prompt, response, tool spans, and token counts behind the label.

Apply this. For the SRE agent the questions that matter: did it identify the right pod, call the right tool (not guess), and stay grounded in real tool output (no hallucinated pod names)? The per-metric summary and evals/phoenix/out/phoenix_eval_results.csv give you the same numbers outside the UI.

Go deeper. 06 — Evaluate · Part A (Phoenix).

docs.title: Step 10 — Review the dt-evals results
docs.text:
What & why. The dt-evals run from Step 7 wrote its scores into Dynatrace as bizevents. Read them with DQL — this is the queryable, alertable, CI-gated view of quality.

Do it. In a Dynatrace Notebook:

fetch bizevents
| filter event.type == "gen_ai.evaluation.result"
| summarize avg(toDouble(gen_ai.evaluation.score.value)), by: { gen_ai.evaluation.name }

Apply this. You get an average score per evaluator (relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, …). Because the scores live next to the spans, any low score is one click from the trace, prompt, and tool calls that produced it — and the run already exited non-zero if a threshold was breached, which is your CI gate.

Go deeper. 06 — Evaluate · Part B · Read the scores.

docs.title: Step 11 — Deploy the notebook
docs.text:
What & why. You've measured cost (Step 6) and quality (Steps 9–10). The optimize module ships a ready-made Dynatrace notebook that computes every optimization signal from your crew's gen_ai.* spans — deploy it so the next DQL steps run against a real surface, not a blank page.

Do it.

dtctl config use-context <your-tenant>
cd cluster/dynatrace/optimization
dtctl create notebook -f ai-agent-optimization-before-after.notebook.yaml

Apply this. The notebook — AI Agent Optimization — before/after — is the observe → find → change → re-measure → keep/revert walkthrough, one runnable DQL cell per step. Its §5 cell measures the single number optimization moves: average input tokens per call_llm. (The companion dashboard, ai-agent-optimization.dashboard.yaml, deploys the same way with dtctl apply -f.)

Go deeper. 07 — Optimize · deploy the surfaces.

docs.title: Step 12 — Build DQL queries: tool usage + token utilization
docs.text:
What & why. This is the heart of optimization. Two questions answer "where is the waste?": which tools does an agent actually call (anything granted but never called is pure prompt overhead), and how many tokens is each agent burning (especially the input:output ratio, your waste compass).

Do it — token utilization (rank agents by spend):

fetch spans
| filter service.namespace == "kagent" and isNotNull(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens)
| summarize llmCalls = count(),
    inputTokens  = sum(gen_ai.usage.input_tokens),
    outputTokens = sum(gen_ai.usage.output_tokens),
    by:{agent = service.name}
| fieldsAdd totalTokens = inputTokens + outputTokens,
    inOutRatio      = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / outputTokens, decimals: 1),
    avgInputPerCall = round(toDouble(inputTokens) / llmCalls)
| sort totalTokens desc

Do it — tool usage (what an agent really calls):

fetch spans
| filter service.namespace == "kagent" and service.name == "<agent-service-name>"
    and gen_ai.operation.name == "execute_tool" and gen_ai.tool.name != "(merged tools)"
| summarize calls = count(), by:{tool = gen_ai.tool.name}
| sort calls desc

Apply this. Diff the tools the traces prove an agent uses against the tool set it was granted — every unused tool is a JSON schema injected into every prompt (~165 input tokens per tool, on every call). A high input:output ratio (e.g. 38:1) means the model re-reads a large context each call — that, not the raw total, is where to cut. This ranking is the raw material for the cuts in module 07.

Go deeper. 07 — Optimize · the four cuts.

docs.title: Step 13 — Deploy the workflow
docs.text:
What & why. Optimization isn't a one-off. Because cost and quality are now both telemetry, the last artifact makes the loop continuous: a scheduled Dynatrace workflow runs a Site Reliability Guardian daily, so a cost or quality regression fails loudly on its own.

Do it. Deploy the guardian, then the workflow that runs it:

cd cluster/dynatrace/optimization
dtctl create settings -f ai-agent-quality-cost.guardian.yaml \
  --schema app:dynatrace.site.reliability.guardian:guardians --scope environment
dtctl create workflow -f ai-agent-optimization.workflow.yaml

Apply this. The guardian holds three DQL objectives over the crew's call_llm spans — cost per call (avg input tokens ≤ 20k), loop efficiency (avg hops ≤ 5), and an answer-substance quality proxy (avg output tokens ≥ 200) so an agent that got "cheaper" by truncating answers trips the gate. The workflow ships with its schedule disabled; flip trigger.schedule.isActive: true to run it over the last 24h every day.

Go deeper. 07 — Optimize · make it continuous.

docs.title: You've run the whole show
docs.text: In thirteen steps you configured an agent, investigated a cluster, exposed the telemetry pipeline, evaluated the results two ways, and closed the observe → evaluate → optimize loop with queries and automation that keep the crew cost-efficient. For the depth behind any step, follow its Go deeper link — and when something misbehaves, the Troubleshooting page collects the common fixes per module.

docs.title: Start the benchmark
docs.text:
This is the front door to the workshop. Follow it top to bottom and you go from nothing to a running cluster with every token in place — without reading any other page first. It is also the single source of truth for secrets: every later module links back here instead of re-listing tokens.

The whole path is four steps:

flowchart LR
  A[1. Fork the repo] --> B[2. Create a Codespace<br/>on YOUR fork]
  B --> C[3. Add Codespace secrets]
  C --> D[4. Create the 5 tokens<br/>with the right scopes]
  D --> E[Rebuild / open Codespace<br/>cluster comes up automatically]

You will need accounts on three services before you start:

  • GitHub (free) — to fork and run the Codespace.
  • Dynatrace — a tenant you can create tokens in. A free Dynatrace trial works.
  • DeepSeek — for the LLM key that powers the agents (platform.deepseek.com).

docs.title: 1. Fork the repo
docs.text:
Create your own copy of the workshop repository under your GitHub account.

  1. Open the workshop repo: henrikrexed/dynatrace-AI-Agent-Workshop.
  2. Click Fork (top-right) → Create fork. Keep the default name.

You now have your-username/dynatrace-AI-Agent-Workshop. Everything below happens on your fork, never on the upstream repo.

Why fork?

The published workshop site and the demo write-back (issues/PRs the BMAD crew creates) run against your repository. Working on a fork keeps your tokens, your Codespace secrets, and your GitHub Pages copy entirely under your own account.

New to forks? See GitHub's Fork a repo guide.

docs.title: 2. Create a Codespace on your fork
docs.text:
The devcontainer installs the full toolchain (kubectl, helm, kind, kagent, uv, mkdocs, …) and, on create, builds a local Kubernetes cluster automatically.

  1. On your fork (your-username/dynatrace-AI-Agent-Workshop), click Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main.
  2. Make sure the repository shown is your fork, not henrikrexed/….
  3. Machine type: choose 4-core / 16 GB or larger. The default 2-core / 4 GB is not enough for the full stack.

Set the secrets first (Step 3) — it saves a rebuild

Codespace secrets are injected at container start. If you create the Codespace before adding them, add the secrets, then run Codespaces: Rebuild Container so the values are picked up.

docs.title: 3. Add your Codespace secrets
docs.text:
Set the tokens from Step 4 as Codespace secrets so they are injected as environment variables — never committed to git.

  1. Go to GitHub Settings → Codespaces → Secrets (github.com/settings/codespaces), or your fork's Settings → Secrets and variables → Codespaces for a repo-scoped secret.
  2. For each secret in the table below, click New secret, paste the value, and scope it to your fork (your-username/dynatrace-AI-Agent-Workshop).
  3. After adding or rotating a secret, rebuild or restart the Codespace.

GitHub only prompts for the declared variables in the Create codespace with options… dialog; you can also set them any time from the Codespaces secrets page above. Reference: GitHub's account-specific Codespaces secrets.

Secret Required What it is DT_TENANT_URL ✅ Dynatrace tenant URL, e.g. https://abc12345.live.dynatrace.com. DT_API_TOKEN ✅ Dynatrace OTLP ingest token (dt0c01) — see token A below. DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN ✅ Dynatrace platform token (dt0s16) for the SRE MCP + dtctl — token B. DYNATRACE_API_TOKEN ✅ Dedicated dt-evals token (dt0c01) — token C. Distinct from DT_API_TOKEN. DEEPSEEK_API_KEY ✅ DeepSeek LLM key powering the agents — token D. (Fallback var: LLM_API_KEY.) GH_PAT ✅ GitHub fine-grained PAT for the demo write-back — token E. GH_DEMO_REPO ✅ The demo repo the GitHub MCP writes to, as owner/repo (e.g. your-username/bad-crew-demo). DT_ENVIRONMENT optional Dynatrace apps URL (https://<env>.apps.dynatrace.com). Derived from DT_TENANT_URL if unset.

Verify presence once the Codespace is up (values are never printed):

bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/check-secrets.sh

docs.title: 4. Create the required tokens
docs.text: Five credentials power the workshop. Create each one with exactly the permissions below — over-scoping is a security risk, under-scoping breaks a module.

docs.title: A. Dynatrace OTLP ingest token → DT_API_TOKEN
docs.text:
Used by the Dynatrace Operator and the OpenTelemetry collector to send the agents' traces, metrics, and logs into Dynatrace.

  • Type: API token, prefix dt0c01.
  • Scopes: openTelemetryTrace.ingest · metrics.ingest · logs.ingest.
  • Create it: in your Dynatrace environment, open Access Tokens (https://<your-env>.apps.dynatrace.com/ui/apps/dynatrace.classic.tokens) → Generate new token → select the three ingest scopes.
  • Docs: Dynatrace access tokens.

docs.title: B. Dynatrace platform token → DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN
docs.text:
Used by the Dynatrace MCP server (the SRE agent's tools: problems, entities, logs, metrics) and the dtctl CLI in the optimization module.

  • Type: platform token, prefix dt0s16.
  • Create it: at My platform tokens → Generate token. The token inherits your user's platform permissions.
  • Docs: Dynatrace platform tokens.

Platform ≠ OTLP

DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN (dt0s16) is not the same as DT_API_TOKEN (dt0c01). They authenticate against different Dynatrace surfaces — keep them separate.

docs.title: C. Dynatrace dt-evals token → DYNATRACE_API_TOKEN
docs.text:
Used by the dt-evals CLI to read agent spans and write evaluation results back into Dynatrace. It is a separate dt0c01 token from the OTLP one.

  • Type: API token, prefix dt0c01.
  • Scopes: storage:spans:read and storage:events:write.
  • Create it: same Access Tokens page as token A, but select those two storage scopes.
  • Docs: Dynatrace access tokens.

docs.title: D. LLM / DeepSeek API key → DEEPSEEK_API_KEY
docs.text:
Powers every kagent agent (DeepSeek is the cost-efficient default for the workshop). DeepSeek's API is OpenAI-compatible.

  • Create it: at platform.deepseek.com/api_keys → Create new API key. Copy it immediately — DeepSeek shows it only once.
  • Docs: DeepSeek API docs.

docs.title: E. GitHub fine-grained PAT → GH_PAT
docs.text:
Used by the GitHub MCP so the BMAD "bad crew" can open issues and pull requests on your demo repo.

  • Type: fine-grained personal access token, scoped to the single demo repo only (the one you set in GH_DEMO_REPO) — not all repositories, no org or admin access.
  • Repository permissions: Contents → Read and write · Issues → Read and write · Pull requests → Read and write.
  • Create it: at github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new (Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token) → under Repository access pick Only select repositories and choose your demo repo → set the three permissions above.
  • Docs: Creating a fine-grained PAT.

docs.title: 5. Confirm you're ready
docs.text:
Open (or rebuild) the Codespace. postCreate runs automatically and builds the local cluster. When the terminal settles, verify:

bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/check-secrets.sh   # all required secrets present?
kubectl get nodes                                # a Ready node?
